reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: A disabling low-frequency tremor that is present at rest and worsens with posture and especially with goal-directed movement
It is typically irregular and coarse, unlike the more regular tremor of Parkinson disease or essential tremor
It results from lesions affecting both the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal (dopaminergic) pathways, often in the midbrain or thalamus
There is characteristically a delay of weeks to months between the causative lesion and tremor onset
Common causes include stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis and other structural midbrain lesions
It is often refractory to drugs, and some patients are considered for deep brain stimulation
reference.pathophysiology: Holmes tremor arises from combined disruption of the cerebellothalamocortical outflow and the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system, usually from a single strategically placed lesion in the midbrain, thalamus or their connections. The mixed damage produces a tremor with rest, postural and prominent intention components, and the loss of dopaminergic input explains the rest component and the partial response some patients show to dopaminergic drugs. The delay to onset reflects secondary reorganisation and degeneration after the initial lesion.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to identify the causative midbrain or thalamic lesion
Characterisation of the tremor components (rest, postural, intention)
Evaluation for the underlying cause (vascular, demyelinating, traumatic)
Assessment of response to a dopaminergic trial in selected cases
Referral evaluation for surgical therapy if refractory
redFlags: A new or enlarging structural lesion
Features suggesting an untreated underlying disease such as multiple sclerosis
reference.prognosis: The tremor is frequently persistent and disabling and often responds poorly to medication, though dopaminergic drugs help some patients and deep brain stimulation can benefit selected refractory cases.
pitfalls: Mistaking the rest component for Parkinson disease
Overlooking the causative lesion by not imaging
Expecting a good drug response and not considering surgery
Failing to identify and treat an underlying demyelinating or vascular cause
